function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script) to finish the whole pipeline.  
I’ll also give you the exact file contents that you’ll need to create/modify.  

> **⚠️ Important** – I can’t actually clone or push to your GitHub repo from here, so you’ll have to run the commands locally on a machine that has `git`, `docker`, `kubectl` and `gh` (GitHub CLI) installed.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# Make sure you have SSH access set up for GitHub
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you prefer HTTPS, replace the URL with `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create the artefacts

### 2.1 Dockerfile

The repo contains a simple Express app (`app.js`) that listens on port **3000**.  
Here’s a minimal Dockerfile that uses the official `node:18-alpine` image (you can change the base image if you wish).

```Dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set maintainer
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> Save this as `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo.

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a single file `k8s/deployment.yaml` (you can keep it in a `k8s/` folder or at the root).  
It defines a Deployment with 2 replicas and a Service of type `ClusterIP`. Adjust the image name/tag to match your CI/CD pipeline.

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- update if you use a different registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **Tip:** If you want a NodePort or LoadBalancer, change `type:` accordingly.

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest

    - name: Deploy to Kubernetes (optional)
      # Uncomment and configure if you want to auto‑deploy
      # uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v3
      # with:
      #   manifests: k8s/deployment.yaml
      #   kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG_DATA }}
```

> **What this does**  
> * Checks out the repo  
> * Builds the Docker image and pushes it to GitHub Container Registry (`ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest`)  
> * (Optional) You can uncomment the deploy step if you have a K8s cluster configured in your repo secrets.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

If you want to keep the `k8s/` folder tidy, you can also add a `.gitkeep` file inside it.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically trigger on the next push to `main`.  
> The Docker image will be built and pushed to GHCR, and you’ll see the new image under **Packages → Packages** in your GitHub repo.

---

### Quick sanity check

```bash
# Verify Dockerfile builds locally
docker build -t nodejs-welcome:local .

# Run the container locally
docker run -p 3000:3000 nodejs-welcome:local
```

Open `http://localhost:3000` to confirm the app is running.

---

## 🎉 Done!

You now have:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight image for the Node.js app |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deploys the app to Kubernetes |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | Automates build & push on every push to `main` |

Feel free to tweak the image tags, replica counts, or service type to suit your environment. Happy coding!
